title: The Leadership Knowledge That Complexity Demands
author: Nick Hart
summary: Hart argues that school leadership is best understood as complex problem-solving, and that the expertise this requires has two very different components: formal knowledge and 'hidden knowledge.' Formal knowledge -- curriculum, assessment, safeguarding law, the science of learning -- transfers across schools and is what leadership qualifications like the NPQ frameworks teach. But because schools are complex systems marked by emergence, unpredictability and historical path-dependence, formal knowledge alone is not sufficient; Hart illustrates this from his own experience of losing almost all contextual expertise overnight when he moved headship from one school to another. Drawing on Bereiter and Scardamalia, he identifies three forms of hidden knowledge leaders also need: informal (pattern recognition), impressionistic (intuition sensed before it can be explained), and self-regulatory (knowing one's own biases well enough to catch them in the moment). Crucially, he argues hidden knowledge is not automatically produced by years of experience -- a leader can repeat the same routines for two decades without ever developing it. The piece closes by flagging that current leadership development systems are good at transmitting formal knowledge but weak at building hidden knowledge, setting up a promised follow-up post on how to build it deliberately.
points: Hart frames leadership as complex problem-solving, distinguishing schools (complex systems marked by emergence and unpredictability) from merely 'complicated' systems where formal knowledge alone would suffice.

He uses his own experience of changing headships over a summer -- formal knowledge intact, contextual knowledge dropped to almost zero -- to argue that school-specific knowledge is necessary but insufficient for good leadership.

Drawing on Bereiter and Scardamalia, he names three types of 'hidden knowledge': informal (pattern recognition), impressionistic (unexplainable intuition), and self-regulatory (catching one's own biases in the moment).
Hart explicitly separates hidden knowledge from years of experience, arguing a 20-year veteran can repeat the same decisions without ever developing it.
The piece positions current leadership-development systems (like NPQ frameworks) as adequate for formal knowledge but insufficient for building leaders' hidden knowledge.
quotes: What matters in school improvement? Ultimately better outcomes for students. Upstream of this is improving teaching, and upstream of that is improving leadership.

When I switched from being the Headteacher of one school to another over a summer, the formal knowledge I possessed did not change. But my contextual knowledge dropped to almost zero over night, making me instantly less expert in my role as the Headteacher in the new school than I was the previous day for the old one.

But schools are complex systems, characterised by features such as emergence, unpredictability, self organisation and historical influence. In such conditions, knowledge of the specific system within which we work is vital.

However a leader can know their school intimately and still misjudge a decision, still miss what's actually driving their own reasoning, still fail to spot a pattern they've already lived through once before. Closing that gap takes something broader than local knowledge.

A leader with 20 years of experience might have done the job for that long without ever developing informal, impressionistic or self regulatory knowledge, repeating the same thought processes and decisions without evolution. Hidden knowledge can be built through experience but it is not a given that experience builds it.
